items.readable_text:
Content:
Terms in a linear expression are called like terms if their variable part is the same. For example, in the linear expression

Content:
[MATH: {\color{blue}2x}+3y{\color{blue}-5x},]

Content:
the terms [MATH: {\color{blue}2x}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}-5x}] are like terms because both terms contain the same variable [MATH: x.]

Content:
A linear expression may also contain multiple groups of like terms. For example, in the expression

Content:
[MATH: 2a + \dfrac{1}{2}b + 3a - 0.4 b - a,]

Content:
we have two groups of like terms:

Content:
- [MATH: 2a,] [MATH: 3a,] and [MATH: -a] are like terms because they all contain the variable [MATH: a.]
- [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}b] and [MATH: -0.4b] are like terms because they both contain the variable [MATH: b.]

Content:
Remember: When a term has a subtraction symbol [MATH: (-)] in front of it, the term is treated as a negative.

[MATH: x - 2y + 11y - 6z - 5x.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We write the terms of the expression as follows: [MATH: ({\color{red}x}) + ({\color{blue}-2y}) + ({\color{blue}11y}) + (-6z) + ({\color{red}-5x})]

We see two pairs of like terms:

  • The terms [MATH: -2y] and [MATH: 11y] are like terms since they both contain the variable [MATH: y.]

  • The terms [MATH: x] and [MATH: -5x] are like terms since they both contain the variable [MATH: x.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Terms in a linear expression are called like terms if their variable part is the same. For example, in the linear expression

Content:
[MATH: {\color{blue}2x}+3y{\color{blue}-5x},]

Content:
the terms [MATH: {\color{blue}2x}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}-5x}] are like terms because both terms contain the same variable [MATH: x.]

Content:
A linear expression may also contain multiple groups of like terms. For example, in the expression

Content:
[MATH: 2a + \dfrac{1}{2}b + 3a - 0.4 b - a,]

Content:
we have two groups of like terms:

Content:
- [MATH: 2a,] [MATH: 3a,] and [MATH: -a] are like terms because they all contain the variable [MATH: a.]
- [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}b] and [MATH: -0.4b] are like terms because they both contain the variable [MATH: b.]

Content:
Remember: When a term has a subtraction symbol [MATH: (-)] in front of it, the term is treated as a negative.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Like Terms

Example Prompt:
List the like terms for the expression
[MATH: x - 2y + 11y - 6z - 5x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We write the terms of the expression as follows:
[MATH: ({\color{red}x}) + ({\color{blue}-2y}) + ({\color{blue}11y}) + (-6z) + ({\color{red}-5x})]

We see two pairs of like terms:

- The terms [MATH: -2y] and [MATH: 11y] are like terms since they both contain the variable [MATH: y.]
- The terms [MATH: x] and [MATH: -5x] are like terms since they both contain the variable [MATH: x.]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Expressions with No Like Terms

Content:
In some expressions, there are no like terms. For example, in the expression [MATH: a+2b] there are two terms, [MATH: a] and [MATH: 2b]. These two terms do not have the same variable part, so they are not like terms.

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Like Terms when there are No Like Terms

Example Prompt:
List the like terms for the expression
[MATH: 20 - 6a + 2b - 6c.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We write the terms of the expression as follows:

[MATH: (20) + (-6a) + (2b) + (-6c)]

None of these terms have the same variable part. Consequently, there are no like terms in this expression.

Item 9 — Tutorial: Constants are Like Terms

Content:
Constants are like terms, even though they do not contain variables.

Content:
To understand why this is, remember that two terms are called like terms if they share the same variable part.

Content:
All constants have no variables, so technically they do share the same variable part. Their variable part consists of no variables at all!

---

Item 10 — Example: Identifying Constants as Like Terms

Example Prompt:
What are the like terms of the expression [MATH: 4 + 0.8p - 2.3p - 3.2p + 10?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We write the terms of the expression as follows:

[MATH: (4) + (0.8p) + (-2.3p) + (-3.2p) + (10)]

There are two groups of like terms:

- [MATH: 0.8p,] [MATH: -2.3p,] and [MATH: -3.2p] are like terms because they all contain the variable [MATH: p.]
- [MATH: 4] and [MATH: 10] are like terms because they both contain no variable.
